stop.more: Stop is the only eight-sided sign, so you can recognise it even from behind or when it is dirty. It is used where a rolling 'slow down and look' is not enough - the view is blocked or cross traffic is fast.
where: Where a village road meets a busy highway
At a railway crossing approach or a blind junction in town

when.s: No other traffic is in sight
when.d: Still stop completely behind the line, look right, left and right again, then move off.

when.s: Your view is blocked by a wall or parked truck
when.d: Stop at the line first, then creep forward slowly until you can see, ready to stop again.

stop.mistake: Rolling slowly over the line without stopping - a 'rolling stop' is not a stop.

giveway.more: The point-down triangle means other traffic has priority over you. Unlike Stop, you need not stop if the way is clearly free - but you must be ready to.
where: Where a side road joins a main road
At the entry to a roundabout

when.s: A vehicle on the main road is close or you can't judge its speed
when.d: Stop behind the give-way line and wait for a bigger gap.

when.s: The main road is clear far in both directions
when.d: Enter at low speed without stopping, still watching both ways.

giveway.mistake: Pulling out and forcing a vehicle on the main road to brake.

noentry.more: A red disc with a white bar marks the 'wrong end' of a one-way road or an exit-only gate. Every vehicle coming the other way expects the road to be empty of oncoming traffic.
where: The exit end of a one-way street in town
The exit lane of a petrol pump, mall or toll plaza

when.s: Your map app tells you to go in
when.d: Trust the sign, not the app - take the next legal route.

when.s: You've already entered by mistake
when.d: Stop safely at the edge, switch on hazard lights and turn round only when it is safe; don't drive on against the traffic.

noentry.mistake: Entering 'just for a few metres' to reach a shop.

oneway.more: Placed at the start of a one-way road and repeated at junctions along it. Two-wheelers are not exempt.
where: Market roads and narrow streets in old town centres

when.s: You missed your turn on a one-way road
when.d: Carry on with the flow and come back round the block.

when.s: You are crossing a one-way road on foot
when.d: Look mainly towards the traffic, but check the other way for wrong-way riders.

oneway.mistake: Riding a scooter a short distance against the arrow - oncoming drivers won't expect you.

allprohib.more: A plain red-ringed white circle closes the road to all vehicles in both directions, often temporarily for repairs, events or a pedestrian zone.
where: Roads closed for a festival, procession or repairs

when.s: You need to reach an address on that road
when.d: Park outside and walk in, or ask the officials on duty.

when.s: A local says it's fine to drive through
when.d: Follow the sign - it is there for people on foot or workers inside.

allprohib.mistake: Squeezing a two-wheeler past the board because 'it is only for cars'.

noahead.more: Usually placed where the road ahead becomes one-way against you, is closed, or crosses a busy carriageway that can't be crossed safely.
where: Junctions where the road ahead is one-way the other way
Median gaps on divided highways that allow turning only

when.s: Your destination is straight across
when.d: Turn left or right as allowed and use the next legal crossing or U-turn point.

when.s: Traffic police wave you straight on
when.d: A police officer's direction overrides the sign - go carefully as directed.

noahead.mistake: Darting straight across when the junction looks empty.

noright.more: Often at busy junctions where right-turning traffic would block the flow or cross fast oncoming lanes. It applies only at that junction.
where: Signal junctions on city arterial roads

when.s: You need to go right
when.d: Go straight, then turn at the next allowed point or use a loop of left turns.

when.s: You're in the right lane by mistake
when.d: Signal and move across early, or go straight; never turn from the wrong lane.

noright.mistake: Turning right anyway when no police are watching.

noleft.more: Used where a left turn would lead into a one-way road the wrong way, a closed road, or across a busy pedestrian area.
where: Junctions where the left road is one-way towards you
Gates of hospitals or schools that are entry-only from elsewhere

when.s: The left road leads to your destination
when.d: Continue and approach it from the side that allows entry.

when.s: A free-left lane is painted but this sign is up
when.d: The sign wins - don't turn left here.

nouturn.more: Turning round here would cut across fast traffic or block it. Look for the next median gap or roundabout.
where: Near flyovers, bridges and blind bends

when.s: You've gone past your turning
when.d: Drive on to the next place where a U-turn is allowed or a roundabout.

when.s: The road looks empty
when.d: The ban still applies - fast traffic can appear in seconds.

nouturn.mistake: Making a U-turn in two or three movements across all lanes.

noovertake.more: Used where you can't see far enough ahead to pass safely: bends, crests, narrow bridges, ghat roads and school zones. It lasts until an 'end of overtaking prohibition' sign.
where: Approaches to narrow bridges and level crossings

when.s: A slow lorry is holding you up
when.d: Stay back with a good gap and wait for the end-of-restriction sign and a clear straight.

when.s: The vehicle ahead waves you past
when.d: Don't go - the sign applies to you whatever the other driver signals.

noovertake.mistake: Overtaking on a short straight inside the restricted stretch.

nohorn.more: Marks a silence zone around hospitals, schools, courts and some residential areas. Noise there disturbs patients, classes and proceedings.

when.s: A pedestrian steps out in front of you
when.d: Brake - slowing down is the safe answer here, not the horn.

when.s: A real emergency needs a warning
when.d: A short warning to prevent a crash is reasonable; habitual honking is not.

nohorn.mistake: Honking at a slow vehicle or a red light inside the zone.

noparking.more: You may stop briefly to let someone in or out, but not leave the vehicle. It often applies only on the side of the road where the sign stands; a plate below may give times.
where: Near junctions, bus stops and hospital gates
Busy market roads where parked cars would block a lane

when.s: You need to pick someone up
when.d: Stop briefly with the engine running and stay with the vehicle; move off as soon as they're in.

when.s: The car park is full
when.d: Find another legal spot even if it's a walk away.

noparking.mistake: Leaving the car 'just for two minutes' to buy something.

nostop.more: Stricter than No parking: you may not stop even to drop someone off. It keeps traffic moving where a single stopped vehicle causes a jam or danger.
where: Flyovers, bridges and fast arterial roads
Approaches to junctions, toll plazas and airports

when.s: A passenger asks to get out here
when.d: Drive on to a place where stopping is allowed.

when.s: Your vehicle breaks down
when.d: Stopping is unavoidable - switch on hazard lights, get people to safety and set out a warning triangle if you have one.

nostop.mistake: Stopping on a flyover to make a phone call or check directions.

nopeds.more: Pedestrians are kept off roads where walking is dangerous, usually because a subway, foot-over bridge or another path is provided.
where: Underpasses and flyovers with no footpath

when.s: You are walking and the bridge is far
when.d: Use it anyway - crossing a fast road on foot is one of the commonest ways people are killed.

when.s: You are driving and see someone walking there
when.d: Slow down and give them room; they may be lost or in trouble.

nopeds.mistake: Climbing over the median to save a walk to the foot-over bridge.

nocycles.more: Cycles are kept off roads where speed differences make cycling dangerous, typically fast highways and some flyovers.

when.s: You're cycling and the road is banned
when.d: Use the service road, a cycle track or another route.

when.s: You're driving and see a cyclist there anyway
when.d: Give them a wide berth and don't hoot to push them aside.

nocycles.mistake: Riding a cycle up a flyover because the service road is busy.

notruck.more: Keeps heavy goods vehicles out of town centres, narrow roads or weak bridges, sometimes only during certain hours shown on a plate.
where: City centre roads during the day
Narrow residential roads and old bridges

when.s: You drive a lorry and the plate shows hours
when.d: Wait until the allowed time or use the truck route.

when.s: You drive a car behind a lorry that ignored it
when.d: Keep extra distance; it may stop or reverse suddenly when stuck.

notruck.mistake: Taking a lorry through 'because the bypass is longer'.

nobullock.more: Slow animal-drawn carts are kept off busy or fast roads where they would hold up traffic and be at risk.

when.s: You drive a bullock cart
when.d: Use the village road or the service road beside the highway.

when.s: You meet a cart on the road anyway
when.d: Slow down, give it a wide berth and don't hoot - animals can bolt.

nobullock.mistake: Honking loudly to make the animal move faster.

nohandcart.more: Push and pull carts are kept off busy roads where they block a lane and are hard to see.

when.s: You push a handcart for a living
when.d: Use side lanes and the edge of quieter roads.

when.s: You're driving and a cart is ahead
when.d: Slow down and overtake only with plenty of room.

nohandcart.mistake: Pushing a heavily loaded cart up a flyover against fast traffic.

nomotor.more: Only non-motorised traffic - people on foot, cycles and carts - may use this road. Common in pedestrian zones, parks and heritage areas.

when.s: You ride an electric scooter or e-bike with a motor
when.d: Treat it as a motor vehicle - keep out unless a sign says otherwise.

when.s: You need to deliver something inside
when.d: Park outside and carry it in, or ask for permission at the gate.

load.more: Protects bridges and weak roads. The number is the total weight of the vehicle plus everything in it, in tonnes.

when.s: Your lorry is fully loaded and may be over the limit
when.d: Don't risk it - take the alternative route even if it is longer.

when.s: You drive a car
when.d: The limit is far above a car's weight; it matters for lorries, buses and tractors with trailers.

load.mistake: Guessing the load instead of knowing it from the weighbridge or papers.

axle.more: Even if the total weight is within limits, too much weight on one axle can crack a bridge deck or road. Heavy loads must be spread evenly.

when.s: Your load is piled at the back
when.d: Redistribute it before the bridge so no single axle is overloaded.

when.s: You aren't sure of your axle loads
when.d: Check at a weighbridge that weighs axles, or take another route.

axle.mistake: Thinking that being under the total load limit is enough.

height.more: Warns of a low bridge, underpass, arch or overhead structure. The height includes anything on the roof - luggage, ladders, water tanks.
where: Entrances of multi-storey car parks and petrol pump canopies

when.s: You have luggage on a roof carrier
when.d: Add its height to your vehicle's and compare before you go under.

when.s: You aren't sure you'll fit
when.d: Stop before the structure and check, or find another way - never 'try it slowly'.

height.mistake: Forgetting the extra height of a roof rack or a raised load.

width.more: Marks a narrow gap such as an old gateway, a narrow bridge or bollards. Mirrors and any load sticking out count.
where: Old town gates and narrow bridges
Bollards at the entry of lanes

when.s: You drive a wide vehicle or carry a wide load
when.d: Measure it and use another route if in doubt.

when.s: Your car just fits
when.d: Fold the mirrors if needed and go through slowly and straight.

width.mistake: Ignoring a load that sticks out to the sides.

length.more: Used where long vehicles can't make a tight turn or bend, such as hill roads and narrow junctions.

when.s: You drive a long bus or a truck with a trailer
when.d: Use the route marked for long vehicles.

when.s: A long vehicle is stuck at a bend ahead
when.d: Stay well back and give it room to reverse.

length.mistake: Trying to make it round 'with a few shunts' and blocking the road.

speed.more: The number is a maximum, not a target. It applies from the sign until another speed sign or an end-of-limit sign. Lower limits are common near schools, towns and bends.
where: Entering a town or village on a highway
Near schools, hospitals and ghat sections

when.s: It's raining or foggy
when.d: Drive well below the limit - the number is for good conditions.

when.s: Traffic around you is going faster
when.d: Stay at or below the limit; keep left and let others pass.

speed.mistake: Braking hard at a speed camera and speeding up again straight after.

endrestr.more: The grey or black diagonal stripes cancel the restriction shown before - such as a speed limit or no overtaking. General rules still apply.
where: After a school zone or road works
At the end of a ghat section or town limits

when.s: A no-overtaking stretch ends
when.d: You may overtake again, but only when you can see the road is clear for long enough.

when.s: A low speed limit ends
when.d: Build up speed gradually to suit the road - not to the maximum straight away.

endrestr.mistake: Treating it as 'no limits at all'.

cahead.more: Blue circles give orders. This one forbids turning at the next junction - usually because the side roads are one-way or turning would block traffic.

when.s: You wanted to turn
when.d: Go straight and turn at the next place that allows it.

when.s: You're in a lane marked for turning but the sign shows straight only
when.d: The sign applies to the whole road at that point; go straight.

cahead.mistake: Cutting across at the last moment to make a turn.

cleft.more: Every vehicle at this point must turn left - straight on and right are not allowed, often because the road ahead is one-way against you.
where: Slip roads that lead off a junction

when.s: Your destination is straight ahead
when.d: Turn left as ordered, then find a route back.

when.s: Pedestrians are crossing the road you're turning into
when.d: Wait for them - turning traffic gives way to people crossing.

cleft.mistake: Going straight on because 'the road ahead looks open'.

cright.more: Every vehicle must turn right here. Right turns cross oncoming traffic, so they need the most care.
where: Junctions where the road ahead is closed

when.s: Oncoming traffic is heavy
when.d: Wait in position, wheels straight, until there's a safe gap.

when.s: A motorcycle could be hidden behind an oncoming bus
when.d: Look past it before you commit to the turn.

cright.mistake: Waiting with the wheels already turned - a shunt from behind pushes you into oncoming traffic.

caheadleft.more: Two permitted directions; turning right is banned. Pick your lane early so you aren't forced to cut across.
where: Busy signal junctions where right turns are diverted

when.s: You need to go right
when.d: Go straight or left and use the next legal turn.

when.s: You're in the left lane and want to go straight
when.d: Check the lane arrows - some left lanes are turn-only.

caheadleft.mistake: Turning right from the straight lane.

caheadright.more: Straight on or right only; left is banned - perhaps the left road is one-way towards you.
where: Junctions with a one-way road on the left

when.s: You need to go left
when.d: Continue and come round another way.

when.s: You're turning right across traffic
when.d: Give way to oncoming vehicles and people crossing.

caheadright.mistake: Using the left turn because 'it's quicker'.

ckeepleft.more: Placed on traffic islands, median ends and around obstructions. Passing on the wrong side puts you head-on with oncoming traffic.
where: Ends of medians and traffic islands
Around road works or a broken-down vehicle

when.s: The left side looks narrow
when.d: Slow down and pass on the left anyway; never use the right side.

when.s: A pedestrian is waiting on the island
when.d: Expect them to step off; slow down as you pass.

ckeepleft.mistake: Going round the 'short way' on the right of an island.

ckeepright.more: Less common: used where the only safe passage is on the right of an obstruction, for example at work zones or on one-way roads.
where: Road works blocking the left of a lane
One-way roads with an island on the left

when.s: Oncoming traffic could be on the right
when.d: Check carefully - on a two-way road give way before moving out.

when.s: Workers are on the left
when.d: Pass slowly with a wide gap.

ckeepright.mistake: Squeezing through on the left because it seems shorter.

chorn.more: Tells you to give a short horn warning where others can't see you coming - blind bends and crests on hill roads.
where: Narrow hill roads with walls or rock on the inside

when.s: You approach the blind bend
when.d: Give one short honk, slow down and keep left.

when.s: You hear a horn from round the bend
when.d: Slow down and keep well left; a vehicle is coming.

chorn.mistake: Long, continuous honking while speeding into the bend.

ccycle.more: A track reserved for cycles. Motor vehicles must keep out and must not park on it.
where: Beside new city roads and lake promenades

when.s: You're turning across the cycle track
when.d: Look for cyclists coming from behind on your side before you turn.

when.s: A two-wheeler is riding on the track
when.d: Don't follow it - it's only for cycles.

ccycle.mistake: Parking a car or scooter on the cycle track 'for a minute'.

hairR.more: A hairpin bends back on itself to the right, common on ghat roads. Large vehicles need the whole width of the road to get round, and you can't see what's coming.
where: Ghat roads to hill stations such as Munnar or Wayanad

when.s: A bus or lorry is coming round the hairpin towards you
when.d: Stop on your side in good time and let it complete the turn, even if it uses your lane.

when.s: You are going downhill
when.d: Change to a low gear before the bend and brake gently on the straight, not in the turn.

hairR.mistake: Cutting the inside of the hairpin to save time - that's where oncoming vehicles swing.

hairL.more: A hairpin bends back on itself to the left, common on ghat roads. Large vehicles need the whole width of the road to get round, and you can't see what's coming.
where: Ghat roads to hill stations such as Munnar or Wayanad

when.s: A bus or lorry is coming round the hairpin towards you
when.d: Stop on your side in good time and let it complete the turn, even if it uses your lane.

when.s: You are going downhill
when.d: Change to a low gear before the bend and brake gently on the straight, not in the turn.

hairL.mistake: Cutting the inside of the hairpin to save time - that's where oncoming vehicles swing.

curveR.more: A gentle curve to the right. Gentle doesn't mean you can keep any speed - at night or in rain, grip and sight are reduced.
where: Highways through plantations and paddy fields
Rural roads following a river or hill

when.s: You're approaching faster than feels comfortable
when.d: Brake on the straight before the curve, then hold a steady speed through it.

when.s: A vehicle ahead is slow on the curve
when.d: Don't overtake until you can see the road beyond is clear.

curveR.mistake: Braking hard in the middle of the curve.

curveL.more: A gentle curve to the left. Gentle doesn't mean you can keep any speed - at night or in rain, grip and sight are reduced.
where: Highways through plantations and paddy fields
Rural roads following a river or hill

when.s: You're approaching faster than feels comfortable
when.d: Brake on the straight before the curve, then hold a steady speed through it.

when.s: A vehicle ahead is slow on the curve
when.d: Don't overtake until you can see the road beyond is clear.

curveL.mistake: Braking hard in the middle of the curve.

bendR.more: A sharp, near right-angle turn to the right ahead. The road may look like it carries straight on, especially at night.
where: Village roads turning round a field or a temple wall
Highways with a sudden turn at a bridge

when.s: It's dark and the road edge is hard to see
when.d: Slow right down; follow the chevrons and reflectors round the turn.

when.s: A side road joins at the bend
when.d: Expect vehicles to come out; be ready to stop.

bendR.mistake: Arriving too fast and running wide into the oncoming lane.

bendL.more: A sharp, near right-angle turn to the left ahead. The road may look like it carries straight on, especially at night.
where: Village roads turning round a field or a temple wall
Highways with a sudden turn at a bridge

when.s: It's dark and the road edge is hard to see
when.d: Slow right down; follow the chevrons and reflectors round the turn.

when.s: A side road joins at the bend
when.d: Expect vehicles to come out; be ready to stop.

bendL.mistake: Arriving too fast and running wide into the oncoming lane.

revR.more: Two bends close together: first right, then the other way. Speed that suits the first bend may be too much for the second.
where: Roads around old buildings in towns

when.s: You can't see past the second bend
when.d: Keep to your lane and slow enough to stop within what you can see.

when.s: You're riding a two-wheeler
when.d: Brake upright before the first bend; don't brake while leaned over between them.

revL.more: Two bends close together: first left, then the other way. Speed that suits the first bend may be too much for the second.
where: Roads around old buildings in towns

when.s: You can't see past the second bend
when.d: Keep to your lane and slow enough to stop within what you can see.

when.s: You're riding a two-wheeler
when.d: Brake upright before the first bend; don't brake while leaned over between them.

ascent.more: A steep climb ahead. Heavy vehicles slow down a lot, and you may have to stop and restart on the slope.
where: Ghat roads and approaches to hill towns
Ramps of flyovers and river bridges

when.s: A loaded lorry ahead is crawling
when.d: Keep a bigger gap - it may stop or roll back slightly when changing gear.

when.s: You must stop on the slope
when.d: Use the handbrake for the restart so you don't roll back.

ascent.mistake: Staying in a high gear until the engine struggles, then changing down in a panic.

descent.more: A steep downhill. Gravity keeps speeding you up, and long braking can overheat the brakes until they fade.
where: Ghat roads coming down from the hills

when.s: Your speed keeps creeping up
when.d: Shift to a lower gear and use short, firm brake applications instead of riding the brake.

when.s: The brakes feel soft or smell hot
when.d: Stop in a safe place and let them cool before going on.

narrow.more: The carriageway gets narrower - two lanes may become one, or the shoulders disappear.
where: Where a widened highway meets an old section

when.s: A wide vehicle is coming the other way
when.d: Slow down and pull to the left early; stop if needed and let it pass.

when.s: You're side by side with another vehicle
when.d: Ease off and let it merge ahead rather than racing for the gap.

narrow.mistake: Speeding up to get through before the oncoming vehicle.

widen.more: The road becomes wider - often from two lanes to four. Vehicles behind may start overtaking and others may change lanes.
where: Start of a four-lane section on a highway

when.s: Faster vehicles want to pass
when.d: Keep left and hold a steady line.

when.s: Lanes aren't marked yet
when.d: Stay predictable; don't drift into the middle.

widen.mistake: Swinging out to overtake before the extra lane has actually started.

bridge.more: The bridge is narrower than the road leading to it, so vehicles must squeeze in, and there's no shoulder to escape to.
where: Old bridges over rivers and canals

when.s: A bus is already on the bridge coming towards you
when.d: Wait before the bridge until it's off.

when.s: You're both arriving at the same time
when.d: Slow down; the vehicle nearer the bridge or with the clearer path usually goes first - don't race.

bridge.mistake: Overtaking on the approach to the bridge.

sideR.more: A minor road joins from the right. You have priority, but drivers coming out may not see you or may misjudge your speed.
where: Village roads joining a state highway
Lanes coming out between shops and houses

when.s: A vehicle is waiting at the side road
when.d: Ease off and cover the brake; be ready if it pulls out.

when.s: You want to overtake near the junction
when.d: Don't - a vehicle may turn out or in just as you're alongside.

sideR.mistake: Holding full speed because you 'have priority'.

sideL.more: A minor road joins from the left. You have priority, but drivers coming out may not see you or may misjudge your speed.
where: Village roads joining a state highway
Lanes coming out between shops and houses

when.s: A vehicle is waiting at the side road
when.d: Ease off and cover the brake; be ready if it pulls out.

when.s: You want to overtake near the junction
when.d: Don't - a vehicle may turn out or in just as you're alongside.

sideL.mistake: Holding full speed because you 'have priority'.

tj.more: Your road ends ahead and you must turn left or right. At night the end of the road can come up suddenly.
where: Where a village road ends at a highway
Ends of roads in towns and beside rivers

when.s: You don't know which way to turn
when.d: Slow down early and read the direction board before the junction.

when.s: Traffic on the road ahead has priority
when.d: Stop if needed and wait for a safe gap.

tj.mistake: Arriving fast at night and overshooting into the road ahead.

yj.more: The road splits in two. The fork can be hard to read at speed, and drivers who chose late swerve across.
where: Splits at the foot of a flyover

when.s: You aren't sure which branch to take
when.d: Choose early from the signboards; if you miss it, carry on and turn round safely later.

when.s: A vehicle ahead hesitates at the fork
when.d: Hold back; it may cut across in front of you.

yj.mistake: Changing your mind at the nose of the fork.

stag.more: Two side roads join a short distance apart on opposite sides, so vehicles may cross your road in two steps.

when.s: A vehicle comes out of the first side road
when.d: Expect it to cross straight over into the second; slow down.

when.s: You're turning between the two roads
when.d: Signal clearly and check both ways twice.

stag.mistake: Watching only one side and missing the vehicle from the other.

crossRd.more: A four-way junction without signals. Many crashes happen here because each driver assumes the other will stop.

when.s: You think you have priority
when.d: Slow down anyway and look both ways - the other driver may not agree.

when.s: Hedges or buildings hide the side roads
when.d: Approach slowly enough to stop.

crossRd.mistake: Crossing at full speed because the road you're on looks bigger.

round.more: Traffic goes round clockwise (to the left) and vehicles already on the roundabout have priority over those entering.

when.s: You're going right (the third exit)
when.d: Approach in the right lane, keep to the inside, and move out after the exit before yours, signalling left.

when.s: A bus is going round beside you
when.d: Don't ride alongside it - let it exit first.

round.mistake: Entering without looking right, or stopping on the roundabout to read signs.

major.more: Your road meets a bigger, busier road that has priority. Expect fast traffic from both sides.
where: Village roads meeting a national highway
Service roads joining a main road

when.s: Traffic on the major road is fast and continuous
when.d: Wait patiently for a safe gap; don't edge out into it.

when.s: You need to cross the major road
when.d: Make sure both directions are clear, or turn and use a proper crossing point.

major.mistake: Pulling out because 'they'll slow down for me'.

dip.more: A sudden dip, often where a stream crosses the road. A car in the dip is hidden from view, and the bump at the bottom can unsettle the vehicle.
where: Causeways across streams on rural roads

when.s: You can't see the bottom of the dip
when.d: Slow down and keep left - an oncoming vehicle may be hidden there.

when.s: Water is lying in the dip
when.d: Check the depth before you go in; don't go into flowing water.

hump.more: A speed breaker or raised hump ahead. Many aren't painted, so this sign may be your only warning.
where: Outside schools, hospitals and junctions in villages
Entries to housing colonies and campuses

when.s: You're on a two-wheeler with a pillion
when.d: Slow right down and cross it straight, standing slightly on the footrests if needed.

when.s: The vehicle ahead brakes suddenly for the hump
when.d: Keep enough gap that you don't have to brake hard too.

hump.mistake: Swerving to the edge of the road to dodge the hump.

slip.more: The surface may lose grip, especially in the first rain after a dry spell when oil and dust float up, or where mud or leaves lie.
where: Approaches to fuel stations and markets

when.s: It has just started raining
when.d: Double your following gap and brake, accelerate and steer gently.

when.s: The car starts to slide
when.d: Ease off the accelerator, look where you want to go and steer smoothly; don't slam the brakes.

slip.mistake: Braking hard and turning at the same time.

gravel.more: Loose chips on the surface reduce grip and get flung up by tyres, cracking windscreens and hurting riders.

when.s: You're following another vehicle
when.d: Drop well back so stones from its tyres don't hit you.

when.s: You're riding a two-wheeler
when.d: Slow down before bends and avoid sudden braking; the front tyre can wash out.

gravel.mistake: Overtaking and spraying stones at the vehicle you pass.

rocks.more: Rocks can fall from a cutting or slope, especially during and after heavy rain. They may already be lying on the road.

when.s: You see small stones trickling down
when.d: Don't stop below the slope; drive on carefully and report it if it's serious.

when.s: A rock is lying in your lane round a bend
when.d: Slow enough on these stretches to stop or steer round safely.

rocks.mistake: Stopping under the cliff to take photographs.

cattle.more: Cows, buffaloes or goats are often on or beside the road, especially near villages, at dusk and on market days. Animals move unpredictably.
where: Village roads and highways through farmland
Near dairy farms and cattle markets

when.s: Animals are standing in the road
when.d: Slow to walking pace and pass with a wide gap; wait if they block the road.

when.s: It's dusk or dark
when.d: Slow down - dark animals are very hard to see and their eyes may not reflect.

cattle.mistake: Honking loudly - startled animals may run into your path.

pedx.more: Warns of a zebra crossing ahead that you may not see yet - over a crest, round a bend or in busy streets.
where: Town roads near bus stops and markets

when.s: People are waiting at the kerb
when.d: Slow down and stop to let them cross; don't wave them out into another lane's traffic.

when.s: A vehicle has stopped at the crossing in the next lane
when.d: Assume someone is crossing in front of it - stop too.

pedx.mistake: Overtaking a vehicle that has stopped at a crossing.

school.more: A school is close by. Children are small, hard to see between parked vehicles and may run out without looking - especially at start and end of school.
where: Roads outside schools in towns and villages
Near school bus stops on highways

when.s: It's school opening or closing time
when.d: Drive at a crawl and be ready to stop; watch for children between vehicles.

when.s: A school bus has stopped
when.d: Pass very slowly or wait - children may cross in front of it.

school.mistake: Keeping normal speed because school seems over for the day.

work.more: Road works ahead: workers, machines, loose material and narrowed lanes. Workers often have their backs to traffic.

when.s: A flagman shows STOP
when.d: Stop and wait until you are waved on.

when.s: The lane is coned off
when.d: Merge early and in turn, and pass the workers slowly.

work.mistake: Speeding through the work zone once you're past the flagman.

ferry.more: The road leads to a ferry or jankar - common on Kerala's backwaters. There may be a queue, a ramp and a drop into water.
where: Backwater crossings such as those in Alappuzha and Kochi

when.s: You're driving onto the ferry
when.d: Follow the ferry staff's signals exactly, go slowly, then apply the handbrake and switch off.

when.s: There's a queue
when.d: Wait in line with a gap; don't overtake towards the ramp.

ferry.mistake: Driving down the ramp before the ferry is tied up.

cyclex.more: A cycle track or route crosses the road. Cyclists may come out at speed, especially schoolchildren.
where: Where a cycle track crosses a road in new towns

when.s: Cyclists are approaching the crossing
when.d: Slow down and let them cross.

when.s: You're turning across a cycle route
when.d: Check for cyclists coming from behind on your left.

cyclex.mistake: Assuming cyclists will always stop for cars.

gap.more: An opening in the median where vehicles cross or U-turn. Turning vehicles may move slowly across your lanes.
where: Opposite petrol pumps and side roads

when.s: A vehicle is waiting in the gap
when.d: Ease off and move away from the median lane if you can - it may pull out.

when.s: You want to use the gap
when.d: Signal early, slow down in the right lane and give way to oncoming traffic before crossing.

gap.mistake: Driving fast in the lane next to the median past an occupied gap.

unguarded.more: A railway line crosses with no gate and no gatekeeper. Trains can't stop or swerve, and they are often faster and closer than they look.
where: Rural branch lines and siding crossings
Roads beside fields with a single track

when.s: You're approaching the track
when.d: Stop before it, switch off music, lower the window, look and listen both ways, then cross without changing gear on the track.

when.s: Your vehicle stalls on the track
when.d: Get everyone out and well away at once, then call for help - don't try to restart.

unguarded.mistake: Following the vehicle ahead across without looking yourself.

guarded.more: A railway crossing with a gate operated by a gatekeeper. The gate closes some time before the train arrives.

when.s: The bell is ringing and the gate is coming down
when.d: Stop behind the line - never speed up to get through.

when.s: The gate is closed and the queue is long
when.d: Switch off the engine, stay in your lane and don't zigzag round the barrier.

guarded.mistake: Riding a two-wheeler under a half-closed barrier.

quay.more: The road runs along a quay, canal or riverbank with an unprotected edge and a drop into water.
where: Canal roads in Kuttanad and Alappuzha

when.s: It's night or raining
when.d: Drive slowly, keep to the land side and use low beam to see the edge.

when.s: You meet an oncoming vehicle
when.d: Stop and let it pass rather than moving towards the edge.

quay.mistake: Reversing near the edge without someone guiding you.

cable.more: Electric or telephone cables hang low across the road. Touching a live line with a tall load can be fatal.
where: Village roads with low power lines

when.s: You carry a tall load such as hay, a ladder or a crane arm
when.d: Check the clearance before you drive under; if in doubt, don't.

when.s: A cable is hanging down onto the road
when.d: Stop well back, don't touch it, and report it to the electricity board.

cable.mistake: Standing on top of a load to lift a cable out of the way.

signal.more: A traffic signal is ahead, possibly hidden by a bend, a crest or a flyover pillar. Traffic may already be queuing.
where: After bends or bridges where the signal isn't visible

when.s: You can't see the signal yet
when.d: Ease off so you can stop smoothly if it's red or there's a queue.

when.s: The light turns amber as you arrive
when.d: Stop if you can do so safely.

signal.mistake: Keeping highway speed until the signal comes into view.

bullock.more: Slow animal-drawn carts use this road - they may be heavily loaded, wide and without lights.
where: Sugarcane and paddy belts at harvest time

when.s: A cart is ahead of you
when.d: Slow down well back and pass wide only when you can see far ahead.

when.s: It's dusk
when.d: Expect unlit carts; drive slower and use low beam.

bullock.mistake: Overtaking close and fast, startling the animals.

parking.more: The blue P marks an authorised parking area. A plate may add times, a fee or the type of vehicle allowed.

when.s: The bays are full
when.d: Don't double-park or block the entrance - find another legal spot.

when.s: You're leaving the bay
when.d: Check behind for pedestrians and other vehicles before you reverse out.

parking.mistake: Using a bay meant for all vehicles when you aren't one.

parkcar.more: Parking set aside for cars. Two-wheelers should use their own area so bays aren't wasted.

when.s: The bays are full
when.d: Don't double-park or block the entrance - find another legal spot.

when.s: You're leaving the bay
when.d: Check behind for pedestrians and other vehicles before you reverse out.

parkcar.mistake: Using a bay meant for cars when you aren't one.

parkmoto.more: Parking for scooters and motorcycles. Park in line, on the stand, so others can get in and out.

when.s: The bays are full
when.d: Don't double-park or block the entrance - find another legal spot.

when.s: You're leaving the bay
when.d: Check behind for pedestrians and other vehicles before you reverse out.

parkmoto.mistake: Using a bay meant for two-wheelers when you aren't one.

parkcycle.more: A stand for cycles, keeping them off the footpath. Lock the cycle to the stand.

when.s: The bays are full
when.d: Don't double-park or block the entrance - find another legal spot.

when.s: You're leaving the bay
when.d: Check behind for pedestrians and other vehicles before you reverse out.

parkcycle.mistake: Using a bay meant for cycles when you aren't one.

taxi.more: A place where taxis wait for passengers. Keeping it clear lets them load without blocking the road.

when.s: You want to hire one
when.d: Go to the front of the taxi queue rather than stopping one on the road.

when.s: You're driving past the stand
when.d: Expect taxis to pull out or U-turn suddenly; slow down.

taxi.mistake: Parking a private vehicle on the stand.

auto.more: An auto-rickshaw stand. Autos queue here; prepaid counters are common at stations.

when.s: You want to hire one
when.d: Go to the front of the auto-rickshaw queue rather than stopping one on the road.

when.s: You're driving past the stand
when.d: Expect auto-rickshaws to pull out or U-turn suddenly; slow down.

auto.mistake: Parking a private vehicle on the stand.

rickshaw.more: A stand for cycle-rickshaws, which still serve short trips in some towns.

when.s: You want to hire one
when.d: Go to the front of the cycle-rickshaw queue rather than stopping one on the road.

when.s: You're driving past the stand
when.d: Expect cycle-rickshaws to pull out or U-turn suddenly; slow down.

rickshaw.mistake: Parking a private vehicle on the stand.

busstop.more: Buses stop here to pick up and set down passengers. People cluster at the stop and may step into the road to board.
where: Every few hundred metres on town routes

when.s: A bus is stopped at the stop
when.d: Pass slowly - passengers may walk out in front of it.

when.s: You want to drop someone off
when.d: Stop beyond the bus bay, not in it.

busstop.mistake: Overtaking a stopped bus at speed.

truckby.more: A lay-by where lorries can pull off the highway to rest, check loads or wait out restricted hours.
where: Before ghat sections and city entry points

when.s: You drive a lorry and feel tired
when.d: Pull in here and rest rather than stopping on the shoulder.

when.s: You're passing in a car
when.d: Watch for lorries pulling out slowly.

truckby.mistake: Parking cars in the lay-by so lorries park on the road.

petrol.more: Fuel is available ahead. On highways the next pump may be far away, especially at night or in hill areas.

when.s: You're filling up
when.d: Switch off the engine, don't use your phone, and nobody should smoke.

when.s: You decide to stop
when.d: Signal early, slow down in your lane and pull fully off the carriageway before stopping.

petrol.mistake: Braking suddenly from the fast lane to swerve into the pump.

hospital.more: A hospital is nearby - expect ambulances, patients crossing and vehicles stopping at the gate. It's usually also a silence zone.

when.s: An ambulance needs to get through
when.d: Pull left and stop if needed; never block the hospital gate.

when.s: You decide to stop
when.d: Signal early, slow down in your lane and pull fully off the carriageway before stopping.

hospital.mistake: Honking in front of the hospital.

firstaid.more: A first aid post is nearby where injuries can be treated quickly until an ambulance arrives.

when.s: You've seen a crash
when.d: Make the scene safe, call 108 or 112, and send someone to the post for help.

when.s: You decide to stop
when.d: Signal early, slow down in your lane and pull fully off the carriageway before stopping.

firstaid.mistake: Moving an injured person with a possible neck or back injury without need.

phone.more: A public telephone is available - useful where mobile coverage is poor, such as forests and ghats.

when.s: You've broken down with no signal
when.d: Note your location (kilometre stone, landmark) and call for help from here.

when.s: You decide to stop
when.d: Signal early, slow down in your lane and pull fully off the carriageway before stopping.

phone.mistake: Stopping on the carriageway to make the call.

eat.more: A restaurant or dhaba ahead. A meal break on a long drive helps you stay alert.

when.s: You've been driving for two hours
when.d: Stop, eat light and walk around before you continue.

when.s: You decide to stop
when.d: Signal early, slow down in your lane and pull fully off the carriageway before stopping.

eat.mistake: Parking half on the road in front of the eatery.

refresh.more: Tea, snacks or cold drinks are available - a good place for a short break.

when.s: You feel drowsy
when.d: Stop here for a break; a short nap of 15–20 minutes helps more than tea alone.

when.s: You decide to stop
when.d: Signal early, slow down in your lane and pull fully off the carriageway before stopping.

refresh.mistake: Stopping on a bend or a narrow stretch because the tea stall is there.

rest.more: A resting place for long-distance drivers. Tiredness is a major cause of crashes, especially at night and after lunch.

when.s: You catch yourself yawning or drifting
when.d: Stop here and rest; don't push on to 'just the next town'.

when.s: You decide to stop
when.d: Signal early, slow down in your lane and pull fully off the carriageway before stopping.

rest.mistake: Sleeping in the vehicle on the shoulder instead of a proper rest area.

pedxinfo.more: Marks the crossing itself. People on or waiting at a zebra crossing should be able to cross safely in front of you.
where: Outside schools, hospitals and bus stands

when.s: Someone is waiting at the kerb
when.d: Slow down and stop before the stop line or the stripes, not on them.

when.s: A pedestrian is halfway across
when.d: Wait until they reach the other side or a refuge; don't creep forward.

pedxinfo.mistake: Stopping on the stripes in a queue, so people must walk round your car.

nothru.more: The road ahead is a dead end. There's no way out other than coming back, and often little room to turn.
where: Roads ending at a river, beach or railway

when.s: You're just looking for a shortcut
when.d: Don't go in - you'll have to turn round in a narrow space.

when.s: You must go in to reach an address
when.d: Drive slowly; children may be playing and residents walking.

nothru.mistake: Driving in and making a long reverse back to the main road.

nothruside.more: The side road shown is a dead end; the main road continues.
where: Approach roads to temples, schools or homes

when.s: Your map shows the side road as a route
when.d: Trust the sign; stay on the main road.

when.s: Vehicles come out of the dead-end lane
when.d: They may be turning round - expect slow, awkward manoeuvres.

nothruside.mistake: Turning in and then reversing out onto the main road.

repair.more: A vehicle repair workshop or puncture shop is nearby.

when.s: A warning light comes on
when.d: Have it checked here rather than driving on and risking a breakdown.

when.s: You decide to stop
when.d: Signal early, slow down in your lane and pull fully off the carriageway before stopping.

repair.mistake: Driving on a flat tyre to reach the shop and ruining the rim.

dirnh.more: Green boards are used on national highways and expressways. They show destinations, route numbers and distances, and which lane leads where.

when.s: You see your destination on the board
when.d: Move into the lane under its arrow early and stay there.

when.s: You've missed your exit
when.d: Carry on to the next exit - never stop, reverse or cut across the gore area.

dirnh.mistake: Reading the board so late that you swerve across lanes.

dirstate.more: Blue boards guide you on state highways and other roads; white boards are common in cities and on local roads.

when.s: Several places are listed
when.d: Find yours early and note the arrow and the lane.

when.s: You're unsure which way to go
when.d: Take the safest option and correct your route later; don't stop at the junction to decide.

dirstate.mistake: Stopping in the junction to read the board.

dirtourist.more: Brown boards point to tourist, cultural and heritage places such as beaches, waterfalls, forts and temples.
where: Near beaches, backwaters and hill stations
Heritage towns such as Fort Kochi

when.s: You're following the brown signs
when.d: Slow down near the entrance - visitors often walk on the road and park badly.

when.s: The road becomes narrow and crowded
when.d: Park at the first proper parking area and walk the last part.

dirtourist.mistake: Stopping suddenly on the highway to read the tourist board.

mile.more: Kilometre stones show the distance to the next town and the road type by colour: yellow tops on national highways, green on state highways, white or black on other roads, orange on village roads.
where: Along every national and state highway
Rural roads built under village road programmes

when.s: You need to tell someone where you've broken down
when.d: Read the nearest kilometre stone and the road number - it pinpoints your location.

when.s: You're checking your speedometer
when.d: Time yourself between two stones as a rough check.

mile.mistake: Not knowing where you are when calling for help.

centreBroken.more: Short dashes with long gaps divide two-way traffic where you can see far enough to overtake. Dashes get longer and closer as a hazard approaches.

when.s: You want to overtake a slow vehicle
when.d: Check far ahead, signal, overtake briskly and return to your side well before oncoming traffic.

when.s: The dashes become longer and closer together
when.d: A hazard is coming - don't start an overtake now.

centreBroken.mistake: Driving along the centre line instead of on your side.

centreSolid.more: A continuous centre line where overtaking is unsafe - bends, crests, junction approaches and bridges.
where: Approaches to bends and hill crests

when.s: A slow vehicle is ahead
when.d: Stay behind until the line becomes broken again.

when.s: A parked vehicle blocks your side
when.d: You may pass it if the road is clear, crossing the line only as much as needed.

centreSolid.mistake: Overtaking across the solid line because the road 'looks clear'.

centreDouble.more: Two solid lines act as a barrier between opposing traffic, on the most dangerous stretches.
where: Busy multi-lane roads without a median

when.s: You want to turn right into a gate
when.d: Go on to a place where the line is broken or a U-turn is allowed.

when.s: A vehicle ahead breaks down
when.d: Wait or pass only with great care if police or circumstances leave no choice.

centreDouble.mistake: Treating double lines like a single broken line.

centreMixed.more: A solid and a broken line side by side. Each direction reads the line nearest to it.
where: Hill roads where visibility differs in each direction

when.s: The broken line is on your side
when.d: You may overtake if it's safe, and must finish before the solid line resumes.

when.s: The solid line is on your side
when.d: Don't cross it, even though oncoming drivers may cross theirs.

centreMixed.mistake: Looking at the far line instead of the one nearest to you.

stopline.more: A thick white line across your lane at signals and Stop signs. It keeps vehicles clear of the zebra crossing and the junction.

when.s: The light is red
when.d: Stop with your front bumper behind the line - not on the crossing.

when.s: You can't see from the line
when.d: After stopping at it, creep forward slowly only when the signal allows or the way is clear.

stopline.mistake: Stopping several metres over the line, blocking the zebra crossing.

zebra.more: White stripes across the road where pedestrians cross. People on the crossing should be able to cross safely.
where: Near schools, bus stops and markets

when.s: A pedestrian steps onto the crossing
when.d: Stop and wait until they've crossed your half of the road and beyond.

when.s: Traffic is queuing over the crossing
when.d: Stop before it so the stripes stay clear, even if a gap opens behind.

zebra.mistake: Overtaking near or on a zebra crossing.

giveline.more: A row of triangles (or a double broken line) across your lane at a give-way junction or roundabout.

when.s: Traffic on the main road is approaching
when.d: Stop with your front behind the triangles and wait.

when.s: The way is clearly free
when.d: You may go on without stopping, at low speed.

giveline.mistake: Stopping beyond the line with your nose in the traffic lane.

edge.more: A line along the edge of the carriageway showing where the road ends and the shoulder begins - vital at night and in rain.
where: Roads with soft or dropped shoulders

when.s: You need to stop for an emergency
when.d: Pull completely over the edge line onto the shoulder and switch on hazard lights.

when.s: Visibility is poor
when.d: Use the edge line, not the centre line, to keep your position.

edge.mistake: Riding on the shoulder to overtake on the left.

lane.more: Broken lines between lanes that carry traffic in the same direction. Each lane is for one line of vehicles.

when.s: You want to change lanes
when.d: Mirror, signal, check your blind spot, then move across gradually.

when.s: Traffic is slow
when.d: Stay in your lane; weaving gains seconds and causes crashes.

lane.mistake: Straddling two lanes, or two-wheelers riding on the line between cars.

arrows.more: Arrows in each lane show which directions that lane serves at the junction ahead.

when.s: Your lane's arrow points the wrong way
when.d: Move to the correct lane early; if it's too late, follow your lane's arrow and re-route.

when.s: The arrows are worn or covered by traffic
when.d: Look for overhead signs and the arrows further back.

arrows.mistake: Turning across lanes from a straight-only lane.

hatch.more: Diagonal stripes inside a border separate traffic or protect turning vehicles. Don't drive or park on them except in an emergency.
where: Between lanes at junctions and merges
Around traffic islands and bridge piers

when.s: The lane next to the hatching is queuing
when.d: Stay in the queue; don't use the hatched area as an extra lane.

when.s: An emergency vehicle needs room
when.d: You may move onto the hatching briefly to let it pass, if that's the only way.

hatch.mistake: Using hatching to overtake or jump a queue.

kerb.more: Alternate yellow and black on the kerb marks an obstruction or a stretch where parking isn't allowed, and makes the kerb visible at night.
where: Kerbs near junctions and bus stops

when.s: You're looking for parking
when.d: Don't stop beside painted kerbs.

when.s: It's dark and the road curves
when.d: Use the painted kerb to judge the edge.

kerb.mistake: Mounting the kerb to park half on the footpath.

cyclelane.more: A lane marked with a cycle symbol for cyclists, usually at the left edge of the road.
where: New city roads and smart-city corridors

when.s: You're turning left across the cycle lane
when.d: Check your left mirror and shoulder for cyclists before turning.

when.s: You want to stop to drop someone
when.d: Don't stop in the cycle lane; find a place beyond it.

cyclelane.mistake: Parking or riding a motorcycle in the cycle lane.

box.more: Yellow criss-cross lines keep a junction clear. Queuing on the box locks the junction for everyone.
where: In front of fire stations and hospital gates

when.s: The light is green but the road beyond is queued
when.d: Wait behind the box until there's room for your whole vehicle on the far side.

when.s: You're turning right and only oncoming traffic stops you
when.d: You may wait in the box if your exit is clear.

box.mistake: Following the car ahead into the box and getting stuck when the light changes.

breaker.more: Black and white or yellow stripes painted on a speed breaker make it visible from a distance and at night.

when.s: You see the stripes late at night
when.d: Brake firmly but smoothly before the hump, not on it.

when.s: The paint has worn off
when.d: Watch for the bump in the road surface and the warning sign.

breaker.mistake: Crossing at an angle on a two-wheeler.

studs.more: Small reflectors set into the road surface. In headlights they light up the lanes and edges when paint is hard to see.

when.s: It's night and raining heavily
when.d: Follow the line of studs to stay in your lane.

when.s: You drive over a row of studs
when.d: You're crossing a lane line or the edge - check your position.

studs.mistake: Relying on studs alone and driving too fast for what you can see.

bays.more: White lines mark individual parking spaces so more vehicles fit and none block the aisle.
where: Car parks at malls and offices

when.s: The bay is tight
when.d: Reverse in if you can - it's easier and safer to drive out.

when.s: Your car is over the line
when.d: Straighten up so the next driver can use their bay.

objmark.more: Black and yellow slanted stripes on a post, wall or pier show an obstruction close to the road. The stripes slope down towards the side you should pass on.
where: Ends of medians and narrow gaps

when.s: You see the marker at night
when.d: Slow down and pass on the side the stripes point to.

when.s: The road narrows past the marker
when.d: Give way to oncoming traffic if both can't pass.

objmark.mistake: Passing too close and clipping the obstruction with a mirror.

red.more: Red means stop and wait behind the stop line. Turning on red isn't allowed unless a green arrow or a sign permits it.

when.s: The road looks empty at night
when.d: Still wait for green.

when.s: An ambulance needs to pass you
when.d: Move only as much as needed to let it through, without entering the junction dangerously.

red.mistake: Creeping over the stop line while waiting.

amber.more: Amber comes before red. It means stop - unless you're so close that braking would be unsafe.

when.s: Amber appears and you can stop comfortably
when.d: Stop.

when.s: A vehicle is close behind you
when.d: Brake early and smoothly rather than speeding through.

green.more: Green means you may go if the way is clear - not that it is clear.

when.s: Pedestrians are still crossing
when.d: Wait for them to finish.

when.s: The road beyond the junction is queued
when.d: Don't enter until there's room on the far side.

green.mistake: Pulling away the instant it turns green without looking.

greenarrow.more: A green arrow allows movement only in its direction, even while the main light is red.
where: Free-left and right-turn phases at junctions

when.s: The left arrow is green, main light red
when.d: Turn left carefully, giving way to pedestrians.

when.s: The arrow goes out
when.d: Stop - the movement is no longer allowed.

greenarrow.mistake: Going straight on because the arrow beside you is green.

flashred.more: A flashing red light works like a Stop sign - common at night when signals switch to flashing mode, and at some crossings.
where: Minor roads meeting a main road

when.s: You arrive at a flashing red
when.d: Stop completely, look both ways and go only when clear.

when.s: The other road has flashing amber
when.d: They may not stop - wait for a real gap.

flashamber.more: Flashing amber means proceed with caution - often on main roads at night or when signals are off.

when.s: Side-road traffic may come out
when.d: Slow down and be ready to give way.

when.s: A pedestrian is waiting to cross
when.d: Stop and let them cross.

flashamber.mistake: Driving through at full speed because 'it's not red'.

pedred.more: The red standing figure tells pedestrians to wait. Drivers usually have green at the same time.

when.s: You're walking and see a gap in traffic
when.d: Wait for the green figure - drivers aren't expecting you.

when.s: You're driving and someone crosses on their red
when.d: Slow down and let them clear; your green doesn't make hitting them acceptable.

pedred.mistake: Starting to cross as the figure turns red.

pedgreen.more: The green walking figure lets pedestrians cross. It may flash before turning red - don't start crossing then.

when.s: You're turning and the pedestrian signal is green
when.d: Give way to people crossing the road you're turning into.

when.s: An elderly person is still crossing as it flashes
when.d: Wait for them, even if your light turns green.

pedgreen.mistake: Edging into the crossing while people are on it.

count.more: A countdown beside the signal shows the seconds left on the current colour.

when.s: Green shows 3 seconds left and you're far away
when.d: Prepare to stop - don't race it.

when.s: Red shows 5 seconds left
when.d: Get ready, but don't move until the light is actually green.

count.mistake: Starting off before green because the timer is near zero.

hsright.more: A driver's right arm held straight out, palm forward, says 'I'm turning right' - used when indicators fail or aren't visible.
where: Bullock carts, cycles and old vehicles
Any vehicle whose indicators have failed

when.s: The vehicle ahead shows this signal
when.d: Don't overtake on its right; slow down and let it turn.

when.s: You need to use it yourself
when.d: Give it early and hold it clearly, then bring your hand back to steer.

hsright.mistake: Overtaking a vehicle that's signalling right.

hsleft.more: Right arm out and swung in an anticlockwise circle means the driver will turn left.

when.s: You're behind a vehicle giving this signal
when.d: Expect it to slow and turn left; don't squeeze past on its left.

when.s: You're on a two-wheeler beside it
when.d: Hold back - it may cut across your path.

hsleft.mistake: Mistaking the circle for a wave to overtake.

hsstop.more: Right arm raised straight up, palm facing back, warns that the vehicle is about to stop.
where: Vehicles stopping without working brake lights

when.s: The vehicle ahead raises its arm
when.d: Brake smoothly and leave room - it's stopping.

when.s: You're too close to stop gently
when.d: Check mirrors and steer round only if the next lane is clear.

hsstop.mistake: Ignoring the signal because the brake lights didn't come on.

hsslow.more: Right arm out, palm down, moved up and down, means the driver is slowing.

when.s: The vehicle ahead signals slowing
when.d: Ease off and increase your gap.

when.s: You see a hazard the driver behind can't
when.d: Use the signal to warn them as you slow.

hsslow.mistake: Overtaking a vehicle that's signalling it's slowing for a hazard you can't see.

hsovertake.more: The driver ahead waves you past. It's an invitation, not a guarantee the road is clear.

when.s: A lorry driver waves you on
when.d: Check for yourself that the road ahead is clear before you go.

when.s: You're not sure you can see far enough
when.d: Stay behind; you can't overtake on someone else's judgement.

hsovertake.mistake: Pulling out blindly because the driver ahead waved.

polstop.more: A police officer facing you with an arm raised, palm towards you, means stop. Police signals override lights and signs.
where: Junctions during peak hours or signal failure

when.s: The signal behind the officer is green
when.d: Obey the officer and stop.

when.s: You're already very close
when.d: Stop as safely as you can; don't speed past.

polstop.mistake: Driving on because the traffic light is green.

polsides.more: With both arms stretched sideways, traffic facing the officer's front and back stops; traffic from the sides may go.

when.s: You face the officer's chest or back
when.d: Stop and wait.

when.s: You face the officer's outstretched arm
when.d: Proceed carefully when signalled.

polsides.mistake: Moving off before the officer turns to release your stream.

polgo.more: The officer beckons you forward with a sweeping arm movement towards the body.

when.s: You're beckoned on but pedestrians are crossing
when.d: Move slowly and still give way to them.

when.s: You're not sure the signal is for you
when.d: Make eye contact or wait for a clearer signal.

polgo.mistake: Accelerating hard as soon as you're waved on.

dash_engine.more: The engine computer has stored a fault - anything from a loose fuel cap to a misfire. Steady means 'get it checked soon'; flashing means a serious misfire that can damage the catalytic converter.
where: For a second or two at start-up, as a bulb check
While driving, after a fault is detected

when.s: It comes on steady and the car drives normally
when.d: Check the fuel cap, then book a workshop visit soon.

when.s: It flashes and the engine shakes
when.d: Slow down, avoid hard acceleration and get it checked straight away.

dash_engine.mistake: Ignoring it for weeks because the car 'seems fine'.

dash_oil.more: Oil pressure is too low to protect the engine. Running even a few minutes like this can wreck the engine.
where: For a second or two at start-up, as a bulb check
While driving or at idle, if oil is low or the pump fails

when.s: It comes on while driving
when.d: Pull over safely and switch off at once; check the oil level when the engine is off and level.

when.s: The oil level is fine but the light stays on
when.d: Don't drive - call for help or a tow.

dash_oil.mistake: Driving 'just to the next town' with the light on.

dash_battery.more: The battery isn't being charged - usually an alternator or belt fault. The car runs on battery alone until it goes flat.
where: For a second or two at start-up, as a bulb check

when.s: It comes on while driving
when.d: Switch off AC, music and other loads and drive straight to a workshop.

when.s: The temperature gauge also rises
when.d: The belt may have snapped and the water pump stopped - pull over and switch off.

dash_battery.mistake: Stopping the engine in a remote place - it may not restart.

dash_coolant.more: The engine is overheating. Common causes are low coolant, a leak, a stuck thermostat or a failed fan - often in traffic jams or on ghat climbs.
where: For a second or two at start-up, as a bulb check
In slow traffic, on long climbs or after a coolant leak

when.s: It comes on while driving
when.d: Pull over, switch off and let the engine cool; don't open the radiator cap while hot.

when.s: You must keep moving a short way
when.d: Switch off the AC and turn the heater to full to draw heat away.

dash_coolant.mistake: Opening the hot radiator cap - boiling coolant can spray out.

dash_brake.more: The handbrake is on, brake fluid is low, or the brake system has a fault.
where: For a second or two at start-up, as a bulb check
When the handbrake is up, or while driving if fluid is low

when.s: It stays on after releasing the handbrake
when.d: Drive slowly to a safe stop, check the fluid level and get the brakes inspected.

when.s: The pedal also feels soft or goes low
when.d: Don't continue - call for help.

dash_brake.mistake: Topping up fluid repeatedly without finding the leak.

dash_park.more: The parking brake is applied. Driving with it on overheats the rear brakes.
where: If the handbrake switch is faulty

when.s: The car feels sluggish as you move off
when.d: Check this light - the handbrake may be partly on.

when.s: It stays on with the handbrake fully down
when.d: The switch or fluid may be at fault; get it checked.

dash_park.mistake: Driving a long way with the handbrake half on.

dash_abs.more: The anti-lock system is off because of a fault. Normal braking still works, but wheels can lock in an emergency stop.
where: For a second or two at start-up, as a bulb check
While driving, after a sensor or module fault

when.s: It comes on during a trip
when.d: Increase your following gap and brake progressively; get it checked.

when.s: Both ABS and brake lights are on
when.d: Treat it as a serious brake fault - stop safely and get help.

dash_abs.mistake: Braking as hard as usual on wet roads after the light comes on.

dash_airbag.more: The airbag or seat-belt pretensioner system has a fault, so it may not work in a crash.
where: For a second or two at start-up, as a bulb check
After a seat has been moved or wiring disturbed

when.s: It stays on after start-up
when.d: Book a workshop visit soon; keep wearing seat belts.

when.s: Children travel in the front
when.d: Move them to the back seat until it's fixed.

dash_airbag.mistake: Living with the light because the car drives normally.

dash_belt.more: A front seat belt isn't fastened. Many cars also chime, and rear-belt reminders are becoming common.
where: When you start without a belt

when.s: A passenger says it's a short trip
when.d: Belts are for every trip - most crashes happen close to home.

when.s: The light stays on with everyone belted
when.d: A heavy bag on the seat may trigger it; move it to the floor.

dash_belt.mistake: Plugging in a dummy buckle to silence the chime.

dash_fuel.more: The tank is low - typically enough for some tens of kilometres, but it varies by car, road and load.
where: Hill and forest roads with few pumps

when.s: It comes on far from a town
when.d: Drive smoothly at a moderate speed and head for the nearest pump.

when.s: You're about to climb a ghat
when.d: Fill up before the climb; fuel use rises on long ascents.

dash_fuel.mistake: Running the tank dry, which can damage the fuel pump and leave you stranded.

dash_tpms.more: One or more tyres is under-inflated. A soft tyre overheats, grips poorly and can fail at speed.
where: After a puncture or slow leak
When temperatures drop or after long parking

when.s: It comes on while driving
when.d: Slow down, stop safely and look at each tyre.

when.s: All tyres look fine
when.d: Check pressures at the next pump and reset the system as the manual says.

dash_tpms.mistake: Continuing at highway speed on a soft tyre.

dash_door.more: A door isn't fully latched - it could fly open while moving, and a child could fall out.
where: Moving off after passengers get in
After loading through a rear door

when.s: It lights as you start moving
when.d: Stop in a safe place and shut every door firmly.

when.s: It stays on with all doors shut
when.d: A door switch may be faulty; check the doors are really latched.

dash_door.mistake: Driving off and trying to slam the door while moving.

dash_bonnet.more: The bonnet isn't latched. At speed it can fly up and block your entire view.

when.s: It lights after you've checked the oil
when.d: Stop and press the bonnet down firmly until it clicks.

when.s: The bonnet flies up while driving
when.d: Look through the gap at the bottom or out of the side window, brake gently and pull over.

dash_bonnet.mistake: Closing the bonnet gently so it rests on the first catch only.

dash_boot.more: The boot or tailgate isn't closed; luggage could fall out and exhaust fumes can be drawn in.
where: When the tailgate catch is worn

when.s: It lights as you drive off
when.d: Stop and close the boot properly.

when.s: You must carry a long load with the boot open
when.d: Secure the load and lid, and keep windows slightly open for fresh air.

dash_boot.mistake: Driving with the boot open and passengers breathing exhaust.

dash_high.more: Main beam is on. It lights the road far ahead but dazzles anyone in front of you.
where: Dark rural roads and ghats at night

when.s: An oncoming vehicle appears
when.d: Dip to low beam early, well before it reaches you.

when.s: You're following another vehicle
when.d: Use low beam so you don't dazzle the driver through their mirrors.

dash_high.mistake: Keeping high beam on in town or behind other vehicles.

dash_low.more: Dipped headlights are on - the normal setting for night driving, rain and poor light.
where: In rain, tunnels and heavy shade

when.s: It's raining in the daytime
when.d: Switch on low beam so others can see you.

when.s: You've parked
when.d: Switch the lights off to avoid a flat battery (unless your car does it automatically).

dash_low.mistake: Driving at dusk with no lights because 'I can still see'.

dash_fogF.more: Front fog lamps are on. They throw a low, wide beam under the fog.
where: Dense fog on hill roads and highways

when.s: The fog clears
when.d: Switch them off - in clear weather they dazzle others.

when.s: Fog is thick
when.d: Use them with low beam, not high beam, and slow down.

dash_fogF.mistake: Using fog lamps as decoration in clear weather.

dash_fogR.more: The bright rear fog lamp is on so vehicles behind can see you in thick fog. In clear weather it looks like a brake light and dazzles.

when.s: Visibility improves
when.d: Switch it off straight away.

when.s: A vehicle is close behind in fog
when.d: Keep it on, but be aware it may hide your brake lights.

dash_fogR.mistake: Leaving it on for days without noticing.

dash_left.more: The left indicator is flashing. Fast flashing usually means a bulb has failed.

when.s: It flashes twice as fast as usual
when.d: Check the indicator bulbs at the front, side and rear.

when.s: It keeps flashing after the turn
when.d: Cancel it - a forgotten indicator misleads others.

dash_left.mistake: Signalling only as you start to turn.

dash_right.more: The right indicator is flashing. Signal before turning or changing lanes to the right.

when.s: You're waiting to turn right
when.d: Keep the indicator on and the wheels straight until you go.

when.s: It's still on after an overtake
when.d: Cancel it so drivers behind aren't confused.

dash_right.mistake: Using the right indicator to tell drivers behind it's safe to overtake.

dash_hazard.more: All indicators flash together to warn others that you're stopped or a danger.
where: Warning traffic behind of a sudden queue on a highway

when.s: You've broken down on the road
when.d: Switch them on, get people to safety and place a warning triangle well behind.

when.s: It's raining and you're driving slowly
when.d: Don't use them while moving in rain - they hide your indicators.

dash_hazard.mistake: Using hazard lights to park illegally or to go straight through a junction.

dash_esp.more: Flashing means stability or traction control is working to stop a skid; steady means the system is off or faulty.
where: On wet, muddy or gravel roads
When accelerating hard or cornering fast

when.s: It flickers in a bend
when.d: You're near the grip limit - ease off and steer smoothly.

when.s: It stays on
when.d: The system is off or faulty; drive gently and get it checked.

dash_esp.mistake: Taking the flashing light as a sign the car will 'save' you whatever you do.

dash_eps.more: Electric power steering has a fault or is protecting itself from overheating; steering becomes much heavier.
where: After a voltage drop or fault

when.s: Steering suddenly feels heavy
when.d: Hold the wheel firmly, slow down and stop safely.

when.s: It comes on after long parking manoeuvres
when.d: Let the car rest a few minutes; if it stays on, get it checked.

dash_eps.mistake: Continuing at speed with heavy steering.

dash_glow.more: On a diesel, the coil shows the glow plugs are heating the engine for a cold start. If it flashes while driving, there's an engine fault.
where: Turning the key on a diesel, especially in cold weather
While driving, if a fault is detected

when.s: You turn the key
when.d: Wait until the light goes out, then start.

when.s: It flashes while driving
when.d: Drive gently and get the engine checked soon.

dash_glow.mistake: Cranking the engine before the light goes out.

dash_dpf.more: The diesel particulate filter is filling with soot, often from many short, slow trips.
where: Diesel cars used mostly in town

when.s: It comes on
when.d: Drive for 15–20 minutes at a steady higher speed on an open road so it can clean itself.

when.s: It stays on after that drive
when.d: Get it checked before the filter blocks completely.

dash_dpf.mistake: Ignoring it until the car goes into limp mode.

dash_immo.more: The immobiliser stops the engine starting without a recognised key. Flashing when locked is normal; staying on at start-up means the key isn't recognised.
where: When the car is locked (flashing as a deterrent)
When starting with a different or damaged key

when.s: The engine won't start and the light stays on
when.d: Try the spare key, and keep other keys and phones away from it.

when.s: The key battery is weak
when.d: Replace it; some cars let you hold the key against a marked spot to start.

dash_immo.mistake: Repeatedly cranking until the battery is flat.

dash_cruise.more: Cruise control is holding a set speed. It's meant for steady, open roads - not traffic, rain or hills with bends.

when.s: Traffic builds up or it starts to rain
when.d: Switch cruise off and control the speed yourself.

when.s: You need to slow down quickly
when.d: Brake normally - that cancels cruise control.

dash_cruise.mistake: Using cruise on wet or winding roads, or relaxing your attention.

dash_service.more: A scheduled service is due or a minor fault has been logged.

when.s: It comes on
when.d: Book a service and follow the schedule in the service book.

when.s: It's on right after a service
when.d: Ask the workshop to reset it.

dash_service.mistake: Postponing service for months, missing oil changes and brake checks.

dash_washer.more: Washer fluid is low. In the monsoon, and behind lorries on dusty roads, you'll need it often.
where: After heavy use in rain and dust

when.s: It comes on during a trip
when.d: Top up with clean water or washer fluid at the next stop.

when.s: The windscreen is smeared and the tank is empty
when.d: Slow down until you can clean the glass properly.

dash_washer.mistake: Filling the tank with soapy water that smears the glass.

dash_ev.more: On an electric vehicle, this shows it's ready to drive (silently) or that it's plugged in and charging.
where: While charging at home or a station

when.s: The car is 'ready' but makes no sound
when.d: Watch for pedestrians - they can't hear you moving off.

when.s: It's charging
when.d: Don't drive off with the cable attached; most cars prevent it, but check.

dash_ev.mistake: Assuming the car is off because it's silent, and leaving it in drive.

ctrl_wiperF.more: The front wiper stalk usually has intermittent, slow and fast settings, plus a single wipe.
where: On the right or left stalk behind the steering wheel

when.s: Rain is light and patchy
when.d: Use intermittent or single wipe so the blades don't drag on dry glass.

when.s: The blades smear or judder
when.d: Replace them - worn blades are dangerous in monsoon rain at night.

ctrl_wiperF.mistake: Running wipers on a dry, dusty windscreen without washer fluid.

ctrl_wiperR.more: The rear wiper clears the back glass on hatchbacks and SUVs; it often comes on automatically when you reverse with the front wipers on.
where: On the end of the wiper stalk

when.s: You're reversing in rain
when.d: Switch it on so the rear view and camera stay clear.

when.s: The rear glass is dry and dusty
when.d: Use the washer first so the blade doesn't scratch it.

ctrl_wiperR.mistake: Forgetting the rear window in rain and reversing blind.

ctrl_washer.more: Sprays fluid onto the windscreen with a few wipes to clear dust, mud and insects.
where: Pull the wiper stalk towards you (front) or push it (rear)
Behind lorries on dusty or muddy roads

when.s: Mud from a lorry covers the glass
when.d: Drop back first, then use the washer - wiping dry mud smears it.

when.s: Sun is low and the glass is dirty
when.d: Wash it before the glare blinds you.

ctrl_washer.mistake: Waiting until you can't see before washing.

ctrl_demistF.more: Directs air onto the windscreen to clear mist. Turning the AC on with it clears glass much faster, because AC dries the air.
where: When several people are in the car

when.s: The windscreen mists up in rain
when.d: Press demist, switch on AC, select fresh air and open a window slightly if needed.

when.s: You can't see while moving
when.d: Slow down and stop safely until the glass clears.

ctrl_demistF.mistake: Wiping the inside of the glass with your hand while driving.

ctrl_demistR.more: Heats thin wires in the rear glass to clear mist, and often the side mirrors too. It uses a lot of power.
where: A button with a rectangle and wavy arrows

when.s: The rear glass is misted
when.d: Switch it on; it usually turns itself off after some minutes.

when.s: The glass is clear
when.d: Switch it off to save battery load.

ctrl_demistR.mistake: Scraping the inside of the rear glass and breaking the heater lines.

ctrl_ac.more: Air conditioning cools and dries the air. Dry air also clears misted glass quickly.
where: Snowflake button on the climate panel
Most cars, buses and many trucks today

when.s: It's hot and you've just got in
when.d: Open windows for a minute to let hot air out, then close them and use AC.

when.s: You're climbing a steep ghat in a small car
when.d: Switching AC off briefly gives the engine more power.

ctrl_ac.mistake: Sleeping in a parked car with the engine and AC running.

ctrl_recirc.more: Recirculation reuses cabin air and keeps outside air out - good for smoke, dust and fast cooling, bad for long use.

when.s: You're behind a smoky vehicle
when.d: Switch to recirculation until you're clear.

when.s: You feel drowsy on a long drive
when.d: Switch to fresh air - stale air with rising carbon dioxide makes you sleepy.

ctrl_recirc.mistake: Leaving recirculation on for hours with the windows closed.

ctrl_fresh.more: Fresh-air mode brings outside air in, keeping you alert and the windows clear.
where: Climate panel, opposite the recirculation button

when.s: Windows keep misting up
when.d: Use fresh air with AC on.

when.s: You pass a burning garbage pile or dusty works
when.d: Switch to recirculation briefly, then back.

ctrl_hazard.more: The red triangle button flashes all indicators. It works even with the ignition off.
where: Centre of the dashboard in most cars
Usually easy to reach for the passenger too

when.s: You stop on the shoulder after a breakdown
when.d: Switch it on at once, then set the warning triangle behind.

when.s: Traffic ahead suddenly stops on a highway
when.d: Briefly switch it on to warn those behind you.

ctrl_hazard.mistake: Driving through junctions with hazards on, so nobody knows which way you're going.

ctrl_horn.more: The horn is for warning others of danger - not for expressing impatience.
